list.listitem: Prevent pressure injuries by recognizing high risk patients and situations. C
Avoid further damage from disinfectants such as alcohol, peroxide and iodine. C
Provide a moist environment to promote healing. C
Nutritional supplementation in malnourished patients improves healing. C

background.definition: Pressure injuries, also known as decubitus ulcers, pressure sores, bedsores, or pressure ulcers, are localized damage to skin in the setting of prolonged pressure or sheer. Severe cases involve damage to the skin and underlying tissues.

list.listitem: In a recent systematic review, global point prevalence of pressure injuries in hospitalized patients was 14.8%. Stage I and Stage II pressure injuries accounted for the majority of pressure injuries in hospitalized patients.
A systematic review estimated a cost of $11 billion dollars to care for 2.5 million pressure injuries annually.

Pressure injuries occur when the pressure exerted on tissues exceeds the perfusion pressure for these tissues, leading to tissue death and breakdown. They usually occur over bony prominences but may also be related to pressure from medical devices and other objects.

Immobilization devices for patients with possible spinal cord injury cause pressure injuries in 6% to 38% of patients per a systematic review. Risk factors included longer time with the device and need for mechanical ventilation.
See table for risk factors.
Underlying bony prominences and the hardness of external surfaces causes a variation of pressure on tissues and can result in compromised perfusion by reducing circulation.
Healing and resistance to damage can be affected by nutritional and health status. Damage is related to the amount of time tissues are compromised.
A comprehensive skin assessment should be completed on all individuals at risk of pressure injuries.
Appropriate support surfaces (especially specialized skin protection cushions), frequent repositioning, nutrional supplements if deficient, and skin moisturizers can prevent pressure ulcers. B
Patients with a Braden score ≤13 or who are underweight should receive aggressive preventive care. B
A care plan based on the Braden score and developed by AHRQ is available online. B

Combined European and US Guidelines recommend that all at-risk patients (those who are bedfast or chairfast) have a careful skin assessment on admission. The USPSTF has no recommendations for screening regarding pressure injuries.

Patients with a Braden Score of <16 or underweight are at elevated risk for pressure injuries in the Neuro Intensive Care Unit and a Braden Score ≤12 is high risk for patients in all other ICU settings.
Patients with a Braden score ≤13 or who are underweight should receive aggressive preventive care.
A systematic review found increasing evidence that comprehensive, multi-faceted programs in hospitals and extended care facilities can decrease the prevalence of pressure injuries.

Frequently reposition the patient. Though a Cochrane review found no randomized controlled trials in support of repositioning and no evidence based time frames exist, expert opinion often quotes every two hours. NICE Guidelines recommend doing so at least every 6 hours in adults, 4 hours in children, and more frequently if higher risk.

A Cochrane review concluded that alternating pressure (active) air surfaces may reduce the likelihood of new pressure injury compared with reactive gel surfaces in the OR and foam on hospital beds. it is unclear whether it is better than reactive water surfaces, reactive fiber surfaces, or reactive air surfaces. Foam surfaces appear to be less effective than alternating pressure (active) air surfaces and reactive air surfaces.
If impaired nutrition, provide nutritional supplements and obtain a nutrition consult.
Skin moisturizers are effective, specifically to the sacral area.
Educating healthcare professionals to identify at-risk patients and identify abnormal skin areas improves outcomes.

NICE guidelines recommend that patients vulnerable to pressure injuries and patients undergoing surgery should be placed on a high specification foam mattress. While labor intensive, these efforts appear to be cost-effective.
A Cochrane review concluded that dressings and/or topical agents are of uncertain efficacy for preventing pressure ulcers.

Differential.Differential_Features: Diminished distal pulses, decreased capillary refill, other areas of ischemia
Underlying autoimmune disease or associated non cutaneous autoimmune symptoms or findings
Predominantly on the lower extremities, often associated with ulcerative colitis or Crohn's disease
Lack of predisposing risk factors, worsening in spite of appropriate therapy
Rapidly progressing localized lesion, possibly with acute pain and appropriate history, not typically in a pressure related area or at-risk patient

list.listitem: Pressure injuries are staged clinically (): Stage 1: Skin color changes, texture change, non-blanching, with intact skin , usually over a bony prominence Stage 2: Epidermal/dermal damage—partial thickness only Stage 3: Full thickness dermal damage, adipose visible Stage 4: Full thickness tissue loss down to or involving muscle, tendon or bone Unstageable: Full thickness skin loss with eschar or slough precluding delineation of depth Suspected deep tissue pressure injury: Discolored or blistered due to pressure but before necrosis and sloughing

Caveats Cannot be used to categorize mucosal pressure injuries. Slough and eschar obscure the ability to accurately stage. The depth of pressure injuries can vary based on anatomic location (i.e. the nose and ears with no subcutaneous tissue vs. areas of thick subcutaneous tissues). Blanching may not be visible in darkly pigmented skin, carefully assess changes in tissue consistency, temperature, and color in relation to surrounding skin.
The Pressure Ulcer Scale for Healing (PUSH tool) can be used to monitor therapy.

Patients with altered mentation, altered mobility or altered sensation are at high risk for developing pressure injuries. These patients as well as those with risk factors (see ) should have a thorough skin examination with attention to areas of bony prominences. Consider what position the patient tends to be in and whether they are in a wheelchair, are bedbound, wear prosthetics, orthoses or have poorly fitting shoes. Common areas for pressure injuries include the spine, sacrum, ischial tuberosities, hips, heels, malleoli, ears, and elbows. Stage 1 pressure injuries have skin changes of non blanching erythema or texture changes, but do not have overt disruption of the epidermis. The color changes may be more subtle in darkly pigmented skin. Stage 2 pressure injuries have progressed through the epidermis into the dermis but have not breached the full thickness of the dermis appearing as a blister or superficial erosion. Stage 3 pressure injuries have damage through the full thickness of the dermis and into the subcutaneous tissues. Subcutaneous fat may be visible. Stage 4 pressure injuries have progressed through the subcutaneous tissues with either exposure or damage to underlying muscle, tendons or bones.
It is important to consider that ecchymotic areas adjacent to apparently superficial pressure injuries may signify deeper damage that will soon become apparent as the tissues necrose.
Pressure injuries may track deeply or laterally from an apparently small skin opening.
If the clinician is able to probe to exposed bone in a diabetic foot ulcer, there is a high risk of osteomyelitis.
Diagnosis is primarily clinical.
If exposed bone or underlying osteomyelitis is suspected, CBC, ESR or CRP, blood cultures, plain film x-ray, MRI, bone scan or bone biopsy may be needed.

The Braden Scale assesses risk based on sensory perception, moisture, activity, mobility, nutrition, and friction and shear forces. It is also available in printed form online at https://www.in.gov/isdh/files/Braden_Scale.pdf.
The Pressure Ulcer Scale for Healing (PUSH) tool can be used to monitor therapy.
The ELPO scale consists of 7 components each rated 1 to 5. A score of 20 or higher puts the patient at increased risk for developing a pressure injury due to surgical positioning.
Patients should be screened within 6 hours of admission by trained personnel and when a change in status occurs.
Patients at risk should be re-evaluated daily.
Diagnosis is clinical based on appearance and probing the wound as needed to delineate the depth/stage.
Diagrams, measurements, and photographs may be helpful to document and follow pressure injuries.
Eschar on ischemic limbs and heels should only be removed if there are signs of infection or it is interfering with wound healing.

See for a summary of treatment recommendations. Treat Stage 1 and all pressure injuries by relieving pressure and preventing further damage. C Treat Stage 2 pressure injuries by providing a moist healing environment such as a barrier or hydrocolloid dressing. C Treat Stage 3 pressure injuries by the above measures and either an absorptive filler or vacuum. C Treat Stage 4 pressure injuries by above measures and consider plastic surgery consultation for a vascularized flap.C
Avoid antiseptic agents as they can damage fragile healing tissues (e.g. hydrogen peroxide, acetic acid, povidone iodine, alcohol).
Use antibiotics only if there is clinical evidence of infection and not based on wound cultures, as wounds are routinely colonized with bacteria.

Cleanse the pressure injury and skin surrounding the pressure injury. A Cochrane review identified 3 small studies with 169 patients regarding approaches to clean wounds. A saline spray containing silver chloride, decyl glucoside, and aloe (Vulnopur) was better than isotonic saline, and pulsatile lavage was better than sham lavage. Overall, the quality of evidence was limited.
Elase (a combination product of proteolytic enzymes) was not statistically better than control vehicle in chronic leg ulcer would healing.
Control hyperglycemia if present.
Consider oral pain medication or topical opioids (i.e. diamorphone gel) to reduce pain during dressing changes.

A small RCT randomized 42 patients to l-carnosine116 mg/day, a combination of l-carnosine 116 mg and 34 mg zinc, or no additional treatment. Both interventions had greater improvement in the Pressure Ulcer Scale for Healing score than the untreated group. However, the difference between intervention and control was less than 1 point on the 17 point scale.
Eschar should be removed to further assess and treat a wound if there are signs of infection.
Initially, necrotic tissue removal can be accomplished with sharp dissection or by autolysis under an occlusive dressing.

In small trials hyperbaric oxygen therapy resulted in an increased rate of healing in the short-term, but not in the long-term. Studies were generally of limited quality. A systematic review including six RCTs found that Topical Wound Oxygen (TWO) significantly increased ulcer healing in chronic diabetic foot ulcers.
Therapeutic ultrasound therapy has not been well studied, with only three small trials involving 146 patients. Meta-analysis of these trials found no benefit to ultrasound.
Electromagnetic therapy was not found useful in two RCTs identified by a Cochrane review.
Consider PT referral to improve mobility in bed or chair if needed.
Control edema if present.

Many patients with pressure injuries have impaired sensation or mobility. These patients need to learn to reposition themselves frequently or have a care provider that can do this for them to reduce their rate of pressure injuries.
See for a summary of treatment principles, based on European and American guidelines. NICE British guidelines provide an approach to the management of pressure ulcers in adults and children.
A systematic review of 9 studies with 29,572 patients supports the benefit of care bundles to prevent pressure injuries.

Support surfaces: Low and high tech support surfaces may be used for pressure injury treatment. Low tech surfaces include foam, fluid, and air mattresses, as well as specialized foam mattress overlays. High tech surfaces include low-air-loss beds, air suspension beds, and alternating pressure surfaces. It is unclear whether any particular support surfaces is more effective at healing pressure injuries.

Nutritional therapy: While nutritional supplements, especially protein and calories are usually recommended for those with pressure injuries, good evidence from RCTs is lacking and a recent systematic review cites no clear benefit for the prevention or treatment of pressure injuries.Expert opinion recommends 30 to 35 kcal/kg/day and 1.2 to 1.5g protein/kg/day for patients with a pressure injuries who are malnourished or at risk of malnutrition to improve healing.
A systematic review of 14 studies with 1648 patients found that oral nutritional supplements significantly reduce the risk of pressure ulcers (OR 0.54, 95% CI 0.40-0.73).
Supplements: Small studies found that oral supplementation with 4.5 to 9 grams of arginine, 500 mg vitamin C, and 30 mg zinc has been shown to improve the rate of healing of pressure injuries.
Pain control: Assess patients for pain, and control pain by avoiding pressure, using non-adherent dressings, appropriate support (specialized foam) materials, and appropriate pain medications.

Dressing selection: Overall, the evidence base is poor, with little good evidence to favor one dressing over another. Based on expert opinion, it is recommended that one avoid dry gauze dressings. Dressings should keep the wound bed moist, and remain in contact with the wound site. Consider alginate dressings for patients with exudative ulcers and infected pressure injuries.
Pressure relieving devices: a Cochrane review found a single RCT with 141 patients comparing two mattress systems, but no conclusions could be drawn due to the high number of dropouts in the study.
Human amniotic membrane and extracellular matrix dressings are used in some centers and may help wound healing by providing chemotactic chemicals and a structure to facilitate tissue growth.
Weeks to months based on clinical response, with high risk of recurrence.
Consider hospitalization or long term care facility if the patient does not have a caregiver to assist with wound care.

Consider hospitalization for complicated wounds, i.e. to initiate parenteral antibiotics for infected wounds and osteomyelitis, debridement of necrotic tissue, plastic surgery consultation for vascularized flaps, revascularization of ischemic tissues and wounds not responding to outpatient management.

Wound care teams can be very helpful in managing inpatients and outpatients with complicated wounds to address healing, choice of dressings, patient and caregiver education, supplies and prevention of additional and future skin breakdown.
Use antibiotics only if there is clinical evidence of infection and not based on wound cultures, as wounds are routinely colonized with bacteria.

Early signs of infection in chronic wounds include pain, necrotic tissue, delayed healing, and wound deterioration in addition to the classic signs of infection. When infection is suspected tissue biopsy is the gold standard to identify pathogens causing infection. Swabbing the wound should be avoided, but if needed, the Levine technique may be superior to other wound swabbing methods.

Wound care teams can be very helpful in managing inpatients and outpatients with complicated wounds to address healing, choice of dressings, patient and caregiver education, supplies and prevention of additional and future skin breakdown.
Even with appropriate care and protection, pressure injuries heal slowly. C
Pressure injuries even when healed are at increased risk for future breakdown. Predictors of recurrence include more comorbidities and longer time sitting.B
Monitor patients with a history of pressure injury for recurrence if risk factors such as poor nutrition or continued bed or chairbound status persist. C
The Pressure Ulcer Scale for Healing (PUSH tool) can be used to monitor therapy.

feature.caption: Assessment and Treatment of Pressure Injuries.

tr.td: Skin color changes, non-blanching, with intact skin
Relieve pressure (NICE guidelines recommend a high specification foam mattress), and avoid contamination by soiling and preventing further damage

Implement measures for Stage 1. Also provide a moist healing environment with a barrier (Op-Site) or hydrocolloid dressing (Duoderm, Tegaderm). Change hydrocolloid dressings approximately every 3 days or as they become non-adherent. Debride devitalized tissue within the wound bed when appropriate

Treat by the above measures, an absorptive filler (calcium alginate—Sorbsan, sodium carboxymethylcellulose—Aquacel) or vacuum to help with exudates. Moist healing under occlusive dressings also facilitates autodebridement. Place patient on a specialized mattress, i.e. low air loss
Full thickness down to or involving muscle, tendon or bone
Treat by above measures and consider plastic surgery consultation for a vascularized flap
Observe and measure the ulcer by length and width in mm, multiply the two measurements and assigns a subscore
Estimate the amount of drainage after removal of the dressing and before any topical agent is applied.
Assess the type of tissue that are present in the wound bed.
0 - Closed1 - Epithelial tissue 2 - Granulation tissue 3 - Slough 4 - Necrotic tissue
